newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING - ORTLIEB CHASES VAL GARDENA HAT-TRICK.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING - ORTLIEB CHASES VAL GARDENA HAT-TRICK.

text.p: World and former Olympic champion Patrick Ortlieb could join his fellow-Austrian Franz Klammer on Friday as the only skiers to win three consecutive men's World Cup downhills at Val Gardena.

The burly 29-year-old has won the last two races on the north-eastern Italian resort's famous Saslong piste in 1993 and 1995 while the great Klammer, winner a total four times here, took a win in 1975 and two held back-to-back in 1976.

Ortlieb, whose sights are firmly set on the World Cup downhill title this season as the only major crown missing from his collection, can even dream of making it four wins in a row since Val Gardena hosts two downhills this week.
Friday's race was originally scheduled for the Canadian resort of Whistler earlier this month but it was moved after heavy snowfalls prevented it from taking place.
The second race will be held as planned on Saturday.

Ortlieb is in good shape and his vast experience in Val Gardena -- the piste gave him his first podium finish in 1988 -- may translate into a slight edge over his younger rivals in the Austrian team but he still faces a huge challenge.
The Austrians are on a roll in all disciplines of the men's World Cup, led by the previously little known Fritz Strobl in downhill and Hans Knauss in the overall standings.
Strobl won the first downhill of the season in Val d'Isere on Sunday and was fastest again in opening training.
"The win in Val d'Isere gave me a lot of confidence and I like the piste here," the burly police cadet said.
He and his unrelated team mate Josef Strobl are among the favourites but old hands Kristian Ghedina of Italy and Luc Alphand of France are also staking their claims.

Training times give little real indication of the race outcome, with many racers testing equipment and experience on the classic and demanding 3.4 km piste with its midway "Camel Humps" and tough Ciaslat turn.
Some skiers, including Italian Pietro Vitalini, have suggested that the Camel Humps are a bit too exaggerated this year with skiers flying more than usual off them.

Alphand, the World Cup downhill champion for the past two seasons, is looking for his first victory since Garmisch in February and is Ortlieb's major rival on the piste. He also took his first podium finish here, a third place in 1990.
An added incentive is the fact that no French skier has ever won at Val Gardena since the first race in 1969.
The two downhills have been given added piquancy by Alphand's comments after Val d'Isere when he said he did not like the way Ortlieb sometimes behaved.
The comments caused a minor flurry and Alphand was quick to stress that their rivalry was only on the piste.
Alphand, sixth fastest in opening training and ahead of Ortlieb, should have a smoother race than 1995.
Then, the Frenchman was wearing a new bib to designate the World Cup leader and an official, apparently failing to recognise it, ordered Alphand to replace it at the start.
It was then discovered that his reserve bib -- the only one of all the racers -- had been removed from the hut.

The race coincided with protests against French nuclear testing in the South Pacific and there were suggestions -- raised when organisers said none of their officials was involved -- that Alphand had been a target of attempted sabotage.
